    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: Draining peatlands is responsible for a few percent of our global warming

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (738 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that much of the focus for human-caused climate change is on fossil fuels, which are creating most of our problems.
    • A newly introduced study led by Jevan Yu at MIT focuses on peatlands—environments like bogs and fens where organic matter accumulates into thick layers of material.
    • Industry observers note that because these areas are permanently inundated, any oxygen in the water is quickly used up, leaving the job of decaying all that organic matter to anaerobic bacteria that work much more slowly and don’t digest everything.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that much of the focus for human-caused climate change is on fossil fuels, which are creating most of our problems. But land use change is also a large component of the story, accounting for about one-third of total historical CO2 emissions. Deforestation plays a major role here, but practices like draining wetlands also factor in. Exactly how much of our history of eliminating wetlands has contributed to warming is challenging to figure out. But thanks to new sources of data that measure emissions from today’s surviving wetlands, it’s possible to put a better number on it.

    A newly introduced study led by Jevan Yu at MIT focuses on peatlands—environments like bogs and fens where organic matter accumulates into thick layers of material. Some 600 billion tons of carbon are held in these vast stores of peat, which is more than you can find in all the world’s living vegetation, the researchers note.

    Industry observers note that because these areas are permanently inundated, any oxygen in the water is quickly used up, leaving the job of decaying all that organic matter to anaerobic bacteria that work much more slowly and don’t digest everything. So instead of seeing organic carbon turning into the CO2 gas released by aerobic bacteria, in peatlands, a subset of it gradually turns into methane gas. Methane is an even more potent greenhouse gas than CO2 itself and ultimately gets oxidized into CO2. That means there’s a little trade-off from peatlands—most of the carbon they have is kept out of the atmosphere, but the carbon that does escape does so as methane.

    Many peatlands have been drained by digging ditches that let water flow out to repurpose the land for agriculture or other uses. That lowers the water level, supplying oxygen to the exposed peat and ringing the aerobic bacteria dinner bell. Methane emissions get turned down, and CO2 emissions get turned way up.

    Sources indicate that the researchers used recent studies that measure gas emissions from peatlands to build a global model that estimated CO2 and methane release as the water level drops. The two gases respond differently to a given drop in water level, and CO2 in particular responds differently depending on where in the world the bog is located. Using reconstructions of water-level changes due to historical peatland drainage, the team ran their model starting in 1800.

    In a recent development, the simplest way to represent the climate impact of both CO2 and methane changes was to calculate the change in Earth’s energy budget—the strength of the greenhouse effect, in other words. They calculated the total effect in 2020 at about +83 milliwatts per square meter of the Earth’s surface from the CO2 emissions, and about -9 milliwatts per square meter from the reduced methane emissions, for a total effect of +73 mW. That is 2.7 percent of the total human-caused change in Earth’s energy budget. (With the error bars on all these numbers, it’s 1.8–3.6 percent.).

    Or to look at it another way, it means that around 4 percent of all the carbon that was buried in peatlands is now in the atmosphere.

    It has been revealed that regionally, over half of the total CO2 came from Europe, almost a quarter came from Southeast Asia, and only 14 percent came from North America. The timing is quite different, as well, with the contribution from Southeast Asia only jumping up in the last few decades.

    Draining a peatland only starts the process of releasing carbon, though. So that means past land-use change will still be producing emissions in the future. To examine this, the researchers also ran their model forward to 2100.

    According to recent reports, if peatland water levels were simply held constant from 2020 on, the total change in Earth’s energy budget would nearly double, from 73 to 138 milliwatts per square meter by 2100. Moderate restoration of peatland water levels could reduce that growth, and ambitious restoration could even cause the effect to shrink slightly below its 2020 potency in their analysis. This is a process we can halt if we really want to.

    Sources indicate that but since rolling all the way back to the landscape of 1800 is unlikely, elevated emissions will continue for a long time. That makes this another part of the climate system where change plays out slowly, with long-term consequences.

    Nature, 2026. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11339-0 (About DOIs).

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The ruling junta in the West African nation of Guinea-Bissau announced Thursday that it is postponing elections by two years until November 26, 2028.

    The decision came on the 1-year anniversary of the military takeover in Guinea-Bissau on November 26, 2025. The country is currently led by military general Horta Inta-a, who serves as transitional president.

    Inta-a mentioned in a statement that there was "an insufficiency of the technical, material and financial conditions" to hold the election.

    "It is essential to guarantee effective conditions for preparing and holding elections in accordance with the principles of legality, democratic participation, equal opportunity, transparency and electoral integrity," he stated.

    It has been revealed that the military coup in Guinea-Bissau came three days after a general election last year, with the military deposing incumbent President Umaro Sissoco Embalo. Both Embalo and opposition candidate Fernando Dias da Costa claimed victory in the election, with the military arresting Embalo one day prior to the results being released.

    To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

    West African bloc ECOWAS has urged Guinea-Bissau to transition back to civilian rule.

    Guinea-Bissau is a small tropical Portuguese-speaking nation on the West African coast which has seen multiple coups in its history. The country faces a high level of corruption and is also a key point for cocaine trafficking to Europe.

    According to Washington DC-based think tank Freedom House, Guinea-Bissau is only "partly free" due to military interference in elections.

    Reporters without Borders ranksGuinea-Bissau 100 out of 180 countries on its press freedom index, saying the "sharp deterioration of security for media professionals, combined with political and economic pressure, has severely tested the practice of journalism in recent years.".

    Video game-logging site Backloggd has urged consumers to change their passwords after announcing a security breach. The website's administrator MrProg wrote in a post dated November 25 that "someone exploited a bug in Backloggd to gain access to the site's admin tools." As a result, the infiltrator was able to access usernames, email addresses, hashed passwords and the IP addresses users signed in from. Payment information was not affected as that's handled through Patreon.

    Backloggd admin MrProg mentioned that, while the platform uses "a strong hashing method" to mask login credentials, "weak or common passwords can sometimes be guessed from their hashes." As such, it's best for Backlogged users to change their password for the site and anywhere else they use the same one. (Take this as a reminder to opt for a strong, unique password on every single service you use. A password manager can help handle that, while passkeys and multi-factor authentication add extra layers of security to your accounts.).

    According to recent reports, mrProg apologized for the security incident. The admin took Backloggd offline as soon as they became aware of the situation to fix the bug and lock out the attacker, who also hid games and restricted some accounts. All consumers will need to log back in, and MrProg noted they're reverting all the changes the attacker made.

    It has been revealed that "Your game logs, reviews and lists all remain intact," MrProg added. "I'm presently seeking legal guidance to ensure I handle this with absolute care and will share a full notice with more details soon." The site's operator has "already added stricter access to the admin tools and will continue to commit to stronger security features to help protect your account.".

    Backloggd is a site on which people can log and rate games they play, in a similar fashion to what Letterboxd does for movies. Customers can track their game collection, review what they've played, create lists and follow their friends' gaming progress. Backloggd has been around for eight years and it hit 1 million users this month. A native mobile app is coming next year. Those who back the site via Patreon can now check out a beta version of the Android app.
